subject: chemistry
title: The pH Scale
welcome_lead: From sour lemons to soapy bleach, every solution has a place on the pH scale.
meta_desc: Master the pH scale 0-14 in this KS3 chemistry adventure on acids and alkalis.
final_note: You can now place any solution on the pH scale.

concepts.def: A scale from 0 to 14 measuring acidity or alkalinity.
Soluble base with pH greater than 7.
Substance with pH exactly 7, like pure water.
Very low pH (0–2), e.g. hydrochloric acid.
Very high pH (12–14), e.g. sodium hydroxide.

walkthroughs.body_html:
The pH scale runs from 0 (most acidic) to 14 (most alkaline). The middle, pH 7, is neutral.

Below 7 = acid. Above 7 = alkali.

Stomach acid ≈ pH 2, lemon juice ≈ pH 2-3, pure water = pH 7, baking soda ≈ pH 9, household bleach ≈ pH 12-13.

Skin sits around pH 5 — slightly acidic.

An acid is stronger the further its pH is below 7. An alkali is stronger the further it is above 7.

pH 1 is much more acidic than pH 5. Each step is 10 times stronger.

mcqs.q: What happens to electrons when sodium reacts with chlorine?
options: Sodium loses one electron to chlorine; the resulting Na+ and Cl- ions attract electrostatically.
Positive ions are oxidised at the cathode by losing protons.
Protons move from chlorine to sodium to balance the charges.
Sodium and chlorine share an electron between them.

mcqs.q: At which electrode are positive ions reduced during electrolysis?
options: Protons move from chlorine to sodium to balance the charges.
Positive ions are reduced at the anode because that's where positive things go.
At the cathode (the negative electrode) — positive ions gain electrons there.
Positive ions are oxidised at the cathode by losing protons.
